query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a ~100 nm thick Cr film via physical vapor deposition on the surface of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will, during exposure to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours, facilitate the in situ formation of an adherent, continuous CrTaO₄-rich oxide scale that significantly reduces oxygen uptake compared to untreated samples, without degrading room-temperature ductility (8–16% tensile strain) or high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa).
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a ~100 nm thick Cr film by physical vapor deposition (PVD) under high vacuum onto the polished surface of the as-cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Post-coating, specimens are exposed in static air at 1000 °C for 100 hours; if mechanical load is applied, strain rates in the range of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ are used to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO₄-rich oxide layer at the surface that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: The thin Cr film reacts during high-temperature exposure with ambient oxygen and with Ta from the substrate to form CrTaO₄, an oxide known for its low oxygen diffusivity. This protective layer inhibits further oxygen ingress, thereby mitigating pest oxidation, while the limited thickness of the applied film ensures that the underlying microstructure and mechanical properties remain unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the treated specimens will exhibit a reduction in oxidation mass gain by approximately 50–70% during 100 h exposure at 1000 °C, with mechanical properties (tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength) remaining within ±5% of baseline values.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which under high-temperature air exposure exhibits rapid oxygen ingress (pesting) that compromises its application potential despite its favorable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The protective effect of the coating is expected to hold under isothermal air exposure at 1000 °C for durations up to 100 hours; performance outside these temperature or time limits is not predicted.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the exact diffusion kinetics of Cr and Ta during oxide formation, the potential for residual stresses or microcrack formation at the coating–substrate interface, and the behavior under cyclic or mechanical loading not accounted for in the static test conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens: one group of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples treated with a ~100 nm thick Cr film via PVD, and a control group left untreated. Subject both groups to static air exposure at 1000 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, perform weight gain measurements, surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis using SEM, TEM, and XRD to verify the formation and adhesion of the CrTaO₄-rich oxide scale, and conduct mechanical tests (tensile and high-temperature yield strength) to evaluate any changes in performance.
measurements: Phase identification and chemical composition of the oxide scale (via XRD and EDS)
Thickness and continuity of the oxide scale (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Room-temperature tensile ductility (percentage strain to failure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the PVD-coated specimens do not show a statistically significant (≥50%) reduction in oxidation mass gain relative to untreated specimens, if a continuous, adherent CrTaO₄-rich oxide scale does not form, or if the room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength degrade by more than ±5% compared to the untreated baseline.

In summary, isothermal oxidation at 1000 and 1100 °C was performed on a novel RHEA for up to 200 hours, such long-term oxidation test has not been reported before for this class of alloys. The weight gain behaviours during the tests could be affected by evolutions of external oxidation, internal oxidation, and nitridation. The multiple stages of weight gain behaviour at 1100 °C were never discussed in previous studies since most of them only presented the results of oxidation up to 48 hours,. We believe that CrTaO4-based protection layer and Si addition may be important for future development of RHEA against oxidation and nitridation. However, it is also possible that the growth of a protective Al2O3 or Cr2O3 layer was hindered by prominent CrTaO4-based oxide presence. In both cases, the nature of such CrTaO4-based oxide needs to be carefully examined in the future studies of RHEAs.

papers.title: Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic Hf-MoNbTaTiZr alloys and related subtraction variants (e.g. HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoNbTaTi, etc.)
papers.approach: Subtraction method to isolate the role of each elemental constituent by comparing alloys with one element removed, with analysis of both room‐temperature and elevated‐temperature mechanical properties.
papers.findings: One variant (HfMoNbTaTi) exhibited superior high-temperature performance (27% compressive strain at room temperature, yield strength of 367 MPa at 1400 °C). The study noted that although some variants show promising mechanical performance, further modification either via compositional tweaks or anti-oxidation coatings is required for high-temperature air applications.
papers.mechanism: Elemental effects (solid solution strengthening, melting point, ductility improvements) govern mechanical performance; however, the absence of inherently protective oxide‐forming elements (or surface passivation) leads to insufficient oxygen resistance.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy systems with similar refractory constituents (including formulations akin to Nb-, Ti-, Ta-, and Hf-based systems) where modification of element concentrations (e.g., reduced Ti, Si addition) promoted selective oxidation.
papers.approach: Alloy design geared toward oxidation resistance by promoting a selective surface oxidation that forms a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer; long-term isothermal oxidation tests at 1000–1100 °C up to 200 hours were performed.
papers.findings: The NV1 alloy demonstrated a markedly lower weight gain and improved oxidation resistance compared with other RHEAs that did not form a continuous protective oxide. The study underscored that both the formation of a CrTaO4 layer and the role of minor elements (such as Si) are central to improved high-temperature oxidation behavior.
papers.mechanism: The formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide effectively hinders outward diffusion of refractory metal cations and the ingress of oxygen, suppressing catastrophic oxidation (pesting).

papers.title: New HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by Electrospark Deposition with High Corrosion Resistance.
papers.system: HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy processed as a coating on a substrate
papers.approach: Electrospark deposition (a solid-state processing route) was applied to produce thin HfNbTaTiZr coatings that benefit from controlled, low-oxygen deposition conditions (argon shielding) to enhance surface properties.
papers.findings: The produced coatings exhibited good homogeneity, excellent adhesion, improved hardness over the substrate, and a very low corrosion rate in chlorine-containing fluids. While the study focused primarily on corrosion, the improved resistance suggests that tailored surface processing may also enhance oxidation resistance without compromising bulk mechanical properties.
papers.mechanism: The rapid cooling and protective argon atmosphere inherent in electrospark deposition minimize oxygen incorporation during processing; a fine microstructure with limited surface fissuring leads to improved barrier properties against oxygen.

established: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys as cast provide useful room-temperature ductility (8–16% tensile ductility) and significant yield strength at high temperatures, but their inherent oxygen resistance is inadequate for prolonged service in air.
Prior studies on similar refractory high-entropy alloys have demonstrated that compositional modifications or the application of protective coatings can markedly improve oxidation resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloy compositional modification (e.g. removal or reduction of Ti, or addition of Mo, Si, or Sn) to promote the formation of protective oxide scales such as CrTaO4-based or Al2O3 layers.
approaches_tried.outcome: Certain non-equiatomic variants (e.g. NV1 alloy) showed enhanced oxidation resistance at 1000–1100 °C for up to 200 h, though these studies did not evaluate the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition directly.

approaches_tried.approach: Surface processing/coating via electrospark deposition to form a HfNbTaTiZr coating with low oxygen content and improved surface integrity.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced corrosion resistance (and by implication potential for improved oxidation behavior) without altering the bulk mechanical properties, although this method’s direct effect on high-temperature oxidation in air remains to be fully explored.

mechanisms: Formation of a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale (e.g. CrTaO4-based oxide or Al2O3) that limits oxygen diffusion into the material.
Minimization of oxygen ingress during processing (through rapid cooling and inert atmospheres) that preserves a low oxygen concentration at and near the surface.
Selective oxidation induced by reactive element effects (e.g. via tailored minor additions) to stabilize a protective scale without compromising ductility or yield strength.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize the need for compositional adjustments (e.g. reducing active elements such as Ti or adding elements like Si/Sn) to achieve an intrinsic protective scale, while others advocate for post-casting surface treatments or coatings.

The precise mechanism by which certain oxide phases (like CrTaO4 versus Al2O3) contribute to long-term oxidation resistance remains a topic of discussion, particularly regarding the interplay between diffusion kinetics and oxide adherence.
open_questions: Can a single intervention—be it a minor compositional tweak or a surface treatment—improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without impairing its desirable mechanical properties?
Do the beneficial mechanisms observed in non-equiatomic or coated refractory alloys translate directly to the equiatomic composition under long-term high-temperature air exposure?
What are the optimal processing conditions (temperature, atmosphere, time) for any chosen intervention to yield a stable, self-healing, protective oxide scale on the equiatomic alloy?
opportunities: Investigate a single-step surface treatment (such as a controlled, low-temperature deposition of a thin, adherent anti-oxidation coating that promotes the in situ formation of a CrTaO4 or Al2O3 protective scale) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.

Explore minor surface doping (with elements like Si or Sn applied only to the outer layer) that may trigger the selective formation of protective oxides while leaving the bulk composition and mechanical performance intact.

Conduct controlled oxidation experiments (for example, exposing treated equiatomic specimens to air at 1000 °C for durations >100 h at strain rates similar to application conditions) to directly compare against untreated material, thereby falsifying or confirming the intervention’s efficacy.

directions.direction: Minor alloying addition (e.g., adding a few atomic percent of Sn) to promote the in situ formation of a Sn‐rich protective oxide layer
directions.assessment: Although such compositional tuning has been shown to suppress pest oxidation in some refractory alloys (e.g., Nb-silicide systems), altering the equiatomic balance risks modifying the established room-temperature ductility and high‑temperature yield strength.

directions.direction: Application of an electrospark deposition coating made from a modified version of the Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy with extra oxidation‐resistant elements
directions.assessment: Electrospark deposition can produce a protective surface layer and improve oxidation resistance; however, additional phases or residual stresses might compromise the mechanical performance if not optimized.

directions.direction: Physical vapor deposition (PVD) of a thin, pure Cr film on the alloy surface to enable formation of a CrTaO₄‐rich protective oxide during high‑temperature exposure
directions.assessment: This intervention directly targets oxygen ingress by inducing a protective, low‑diffusivity oxide (CrTaO₄) that is supported by previous studies in similar refractory high‐entropy alloys. A very thin coating minimizes impact on bulk mechanical properties.

directions.direction: Ion implantation of reactive elements (such as Cr) into the near-surface region to modify its oxidation behavior
directions.assessment: While ion implantation can tailor surface chemistry and promote beneficial oxide formation, challenges exist in achieving a uniform dopant profile over large areas without altering near-surface mechanical performance.

directions.direction: Controlled pre-oxidation (heat treatment in a tailored atmosphere) to form an adherent protective oxide scale prior to service
directions.assessment: Although pre-oxidation can generate a stable oxide scale, the risk of spallation and the difficulty in controlling scale thickness and uniformity make this approach less robust than a targeted coating strategy.

choice.direction: PVD deposition of a thin Cr film on the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr
choice.why: This method leverages evidence that controlled Cr addition can promote the formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO₄-based oxide scale (as seen in studies such as PMC6513993 and PMC10142552) without modifying the bulk equiatomic composition that imparts the desirable mechanical properties. A thin (~100 nm) PVD film ensures minimal impact on ductility and strength, while directly improving oxygen resistance.
